title: Use language and communication in occupational learning programmes

lessons.title: Starting your learning programme
lessons.html:
Learning to be a service and repair worker

In a learnership for agricultural equipment service and repair, you learn in the training centre and in the workshop. You will learn about engines, hydraulics, welding, tools and safety. To learn well, you need to use language: listen, read, speak, ask and write.

Know your programme

  • Find out which unit standards are in your programme and what each one is about.
  • Ask your facilitator to explain the outcomes, which are the things you must be able to do.
  • Know your timetable: when you are in class, when you are in the workshop and when assessments take place.
  • Know the people: facilitator (teaches), mentor (guides you at work), assessor (checks if you are competent).

Workshop words

Your trade has many special words. Keep a word book. Write the word, what it means and, if you like, the word in your home language. Some examples:

WordMeaning
TorqueTurning force, such as how tight to do up a bolt
HydraulicUsing oil under pressure to move parts
PTOPower take-off, a shaft that drives implements from the tractor
Service intervalHow often a service must be done, such as every 250 hours
CalibrateSet an instrument or machine so it measures or works correctly

Ways to learn

  • Watch the mentor do the job and ask why each step is done.
  • Do the job while the mentor watches.
  • Read the manual and your learner guide.
  • Talk about what you learnt with other learners.

Never be afraid to say 'I do not understand'. Asking is how you learn.

lessons.title: Reading, notes and questions
lessons.html:
Using information to learn

Reading learning materials

  1. Look at the headings and pictures first to see what the section is about.
  2. Read one part at a time.
  3. Underline or write down new words.
  4. Look at diagrams carefully. Find each labelled part on the real machine.
  5. After reading, tell yourself or a friend the main points in your own words.

Using manuals

Operator and workshop manuals tell you how a machine works, service intervals, oil types and torque settings. Use the contents page or index to find the right section. Check the manual is for the correct make and model.

Making notes

  • Write the date and topic.
  • Use short words and lists.
  • Draw simple sketches, such as how a gear pump works.
  • Number the steps of a job.
  • Keep notes in one file or book.

Asking good questions

Use question words to get the information you need:

  • What oil do we use in this gearbox?
  • Why must we release the pressure before taking off the hose?
  • How do I know when the belt is tight enough?
  • When must this filter be changed?

Working in groups

In group tasks, listen to each person, share the work, and agree who will speak for the group. Disagree politely. Help learners who are struggling; explaining to others also helps you learn.

Language support

If English is not your first language, it is fine to talk about the work in your own language with other learners first. Then practise saying and writing it in English for assessments.

lessons.title: Assessment and your evidence
lessons.html:
Showing you are competent

To earn credits you must show an assessor that you can do the work. Assessment can be:

  • Written: answering questions in a workbook or test.
  • Practical: the assessor watches you do a job, such as changing a hydraulic filter.
  • Oral: the assessor asks you questions about what you are doing and why.
  • Workplace evidence: job cards you completed, logbooks and statements signed by your mentor.

Your portfolio of evidence (PoE)

  • Keep it neat, with your name and ID number on each page.
  • Put things in order using the index.
  • Include signed job cards and logbook pages.
  • Do your own work. Copying from someone else is cheating and will not be accepted.

Understanding instructions

WordWhat to do
ListWrite short points
Name / identifySay what something is
DescribeSay what it looks like or the steps
ExplainSay why or how
DemonstrateShow by doing

On assessment day

  • Arrive on time with your PPE.
  • Listen to all instructions. Ask if anything is unclear.
  • Work safely. Unsafe work can mean you are not yet competent.
  • Explain what you are doing if the assessor asks.

Feedback

After assessment, the assessor tells you the result. 'Competent' means you have shown the skill. 'Not yet competent' means you need more practice. Listen to the feedback, practise, and ask for re-assessment. If you think the assessment was unfair, you can appeal.

Key points

  • Know your outcomes, timetable, facilitator, mentor and assessor.
  • Keep a word book for workshop terms.
  • Use manuals for the correct make and model.
  • Ask what, why, how and when questions.
  • Your portfolio must be your own work.
  • 'Not yet competent' means more practice, then re-assessment.
